newsitem.title: POLAND: Floods put Polish ex-communists on defensive.
newsitem.headline: Floods put Polish ex-communists on defensive.

text.p: Charges of delay and bungling in the Polish floods disaster have forced the ruling ex-communists onto the defensive before September 21 elections.
Eagerly awaited opinion polls from after the start of the two-week deluge may show whether this has dealt the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) a serious blow to its election chances.
The catastrophe, killing 50 and striking more than 1,000 towns and villages, made a mockery of the ex-communists' proud new election slogan: "A good today -- a better tomorrow."

Before the disaster opinion polls suggested the SLD, having held office during four years of economic progress, may be pulling ahead of its main challenger, a rightist alliance led by the Solidarity trade union. This picture may now change.

"The government showed itself completely unprepared, it showed itself unable to take decisions," said a Solidarity chief, Maciej Jankowski, in a view echoed throughout the opposition and much of the Polish news media.

Wide condemnation greeted early finger-wagging remarks by Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, before the disaster's full extent became clear, that ruined farmers should have been insured and could expect no help from state reserves.
"Premier WC demonstrated the arrogance and callousness of a (communist) apparatchik of the 1960s," Wprost weekly commented, and even Cimoszewicz allies admitted it was a political error.

The coalition government of the ex-communists and a smaller Peasant party has since flung resources and personnel into fighting the flood devastation, including hefty pledges of aid for those who have lost homes and crops.
"Whether this will cancel out dissatisfaction over its very incompetent steps at the outset is hard to say now," Ryszard Bugaj, head of the opposition Labour Union party, told Reuters.
Reports from communities hit by floods show many people, justly or not, felt cruelly abandoned by the state as they called in vain for guidance or sandbags to defend their homes.
The ex-communist Cimoszewicz defended his government's actions in parliament and accused critics of making political capital out of the disaster.
